# Completeness Exporter

The Completeness Exporter wraps another logs exporter and counts the log records that exporter
confirmed as delivered, grouped by the pipeline ingestion time bucket carried by each record.
It takes the sending queue over from the exporter it wraps, so that the count is taken after the
queue, at the point where the data was really handed to the backend. Combined with a count of the
records that entered the pipeline, it measures the data completeness of a pipeline segment.

The completeness exporter wraps another logs exporter and counts the log records that exporter
confirmed as **delivered**, grouped by the *ingestion time bucket* each record carries. Together
with a count of the records that entered the pipeline, it gives the data completeness of a pipeline
segment:

```
completeness = otel_completeness_acks_total / otel_completeness_creates_total
```

Across several collectors, divide the acknowledgments of the last segment by the creates of the
first one and the ratio covers the whole path — see
[calculating completeness](#calculating-completeness).

Native collector metrics such as `otelcol_exporter_sent_log_records` tell you *that* records were
dropped, but not *which* ones. By marking every record with a coarse ingestion timestamp as it
enters the pipeline and only counting that marker once the backend accepted it, drops can be
attributed to the minute the affected data was produced, across an arbitrary number of collector
hops, without changing the applications that emit the logs.

## Why an exporter and not a processor

Counting in a processor cannot tell delivery from enqueueing. A processor sees the return value of
`ConsumeLogs`, and with a sending queue — the default for most exporters — that call returns as soon
as the batch is on the queue, long before the backend has seen it. Anything dropped between the
queue and the backend would still be counted as successfully exported.

This exporter therefore **takes the sending queue over** from the exporter it wraps:

```
pipeline → [ completeness exporter: queue → count → wrapped exporter → backend ]
                                              ↑
                              acknowledgment recorded here, after the queue,
                              only if the wrapped exporter reported success
```

The queue of the wrapped exporter is disabled when it is built, so its `ConsumeLogs` blocks until
the backend accepted the data (including its own retries). The queue configured on *this* exporter
provides the buffering and batching the pipeline needs, and it sits in front of the counting point.
The result does not depend on how the pipeline is configured: the count follows the delivery.

## Configuration

| Field              | Default                      | Description                                                                                                                    |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `segment`          | *required*                   | Identifier of the pipeline segment, emitted as the `segment` attribute of the metric. Use a distinct value per collector role.  |
| `exporter::type`   | *required*                   | Component type of the exporter to wrap, for example `otlp` or `clickhouse`. It must be part of the collector build.             |
| `exporter::config` | `{}`                         | Configuration of the wrapped exporter, exactly as it would be written under its own key in `exporters`.                         |
| `bucket_attribute` | `pipeline.ingestion_bucket`  | Attribute holding the ingestion time bucket. Looked up on the log record first, then on the scope, then on the resource.        |
| `sending_queue`    | standard queue defaults      | The [queue][queue] of this exporter, taken over from the wrapped one. Supports everything `exporterhelper` supports, including a persistent queue. |

```yaml
exporters:
  completeness:
    segment: central-collector
    sending_queue:
      queue_size: 5000
    exporter:
      type: clickhouse
      config:
        endpoint: tcp://clickhouse:9000
        logs_table_name: otel_logs
        retry_on_failure:
          enabled: true
```

Notes on the wrapped exporter:

* A `sending_queue` inside `exporter::config` is ignored, with a warning at startup. Move those
  settings to the `sending_queue` of the completeness exporter — that is the queue that ends up in
  front of the counting point.
* `retry_on_failure`, timeouts, authentication, compression and everything else stays with the
  wrapped exporter. A record is acknowledged after its retries succeeded, and never when they were
  exhausted.
* Its configuration is validated when the collector starts rather than when the configuration is
  loaded, because the component type is only known at runtime. A typo in `exporter::config` fails
  the startup with the error the wrapped exporter would have produced itself.
* It reports its own internal telemetry under the component ID `<type>/completeness[_<name>]`, so
  `otelcol_exporter_sent_log_records{exporter="clickhouse/completeness"}` is the wrapped exporter of
  `completeness`, and `..._central` that of `completeness/central`.
* Records that do not carry the bucket attribute are counted under the bucket value `unknown`, which
  makes unmarked traffic visible instead of silently missing from the ratio.

### Building a collector with this exporter

The exporter is not part of the prebuilt distributions yet, so add it to a distribution built with
the [OpenTelemetry Collector Builder][ocb], next to the exporter it wraps:

```yaml
exporters:
  - gomod: github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-contrib/exporter/completenessexporter v0.147.0
  - gomod: github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-contrib/exporter/clickhouseexporter v0.147.0
```

The wrapped exporter does not need to appear in the `exporters` section of the collector
configuration — it only needs to be part of the build.

## Emitted telemetry

The exporter emits two metrics as part of the collector's [internal telemetry][internal-telemetry]:

* `otel_completeness_acks{bucket="<timestamp>", segment="<collector_id>"}` — log records the wrapped
  exporter delivered.
* `otel_completeness_drops{bucket="<timestamp>", segment="<collector_id>", reason="<reason>"}` — log
  records this exporter gave up on, so that a loss is reported instead of only being missing from the
  acknowledgments. The reasons are `send_failed` (the wrapped exporter failed the whole batch, after
  its own retries), `partially_rejected` (the wrapped exporter named the records it could not send)
  and `queue_full` (the sending queue of this exporter had no room left).

The Prometheus exporter of the internal telemetry renders them with a `_total` suffix.

For any bucket, `creates - acks - drops` is what is still in flight. It does not settle back to zero
if the collector is killed with records in a non-persistent queue — see
[surviving a restart](#surviving-a-restart).

To scrape it, expose the internal telemetry:

```yaml
service:
  telemetry:
    metrics:
      readers:
        - pull:
            exporter:
              prometheus:
                host: 0.0.0.0
                port: 8888
```

## Marking the records: the "create" side

The bucket is attached to the records when they enter the pipeline, with a
[`transform`][transform] processor, and counted by a [`count`][count] connector. This half needs no
custom component.

```yaml
receivers:
  filelog:
    include: [/var/log/pods/*/*/*.log]

processors:
  # Must be the first processor: the bucket is the time the record entered this segment.
  transform/completeness:
    log_statements:
      - set(log.attributes["pipeline.ingestion_bucket"],
            FormatTime(TruncateTime(Now(), Duration("1m")), "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"))
  batch:
  # Gives the creates metric the same attribute names the acks metric uses, so
  # that the two can be divided by each other without relabeling in the query.
  transform/completeness_labels:
    metric_statements:
      - set(datapoint.attributes["bucket"], datapoint.attributes["pipeline.ingestion_bucket"])
      - delete_key(datapoint.attributes, "pipeline.ingestion_bucket")
      - set(datapoint.attributes["segment"], "daemonset-collector")

connectors:
  count:
    logs:
      otel_completeness_creates:
        description: Log records that entered this pipeline segment.
        attributes:
          - key: pipeline.ingestion_bucket
            default_value: unknown

exporters:
  completeness:
    segment: daemonset-collector
    exporter:
      type: otlp
      config:
        endpoint: central-collector:4317
  prometheus/completeness:
    endpoint: 0.0.0.0:8889

service:
  pipelines:
    logs:
      receivers: [filelog]
      processors: [transform/completeness, batch]
      # The count connector counts the records the pipeline received, the
      # completeness exporter counts the ones that made it to the next hop.
      exporters: [count, completeness]
    metrics/completeness:
      receivers: [count]
      processors: [transform/completeness_labels]
      exporters: [prometheus/completeness]
  telemetry:
    metrics:
      readers:
        - pull:
            exporter:
              prometheus:
                host: 0.0.0.0
                port: 8888
```

Both metrics are cumulative monotonic sums, so the Prometheus exporters render them with a `_total`
suffix: `otel_completeness_creates_total` and `otel_completeness_acks_total`. Attribute names are
sanitized into label names, which is why the creates metric renames `pipeline.ingestion_bucket` to
`bucket` before it is exported — without that it would end up as `pipeline_ingestion_bucket`.

`Now()` returns the collector's local time, so run the collector with `TZ=UTC` if you format the
bucket with a literal `Z` as above. Alternatively use a timezone independent bucket such as
`UnixSeconds(TruncateTime(Now(), Duration("1m")))`.

Because the bucket lives in the log record itself, it survives batching, re-batching and
serialization between collectors: whichever records end up in a successfully exported batch are
counted against the bucket they were originally stamped with. The counting happens per record, so
merging or splitting batches does not distort the numbers.

The central collector is instrumented the same way, with its own `segment` value. To keep the
buckets of the whole pipeline anchored to the moment the data was first seen, let it reuse the
incoming attribute instead of stamping a fresh one:

```yaml
exporters:
  completeness:
    segment: central-collector
    exporter:
      type: clickhouse
      config:
        endpoint: tcp://clickhouse:9000

service:
  pipelines:
    logs:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [batch]
      exporters: [completeness]
```

### Calculating completeness

**End to end**, and this is the number to alert on, divide the acknowledgments of the *last* segment
by the creates of the *first* one. Every segment stamps its creates from what actually arrived, so
this ratio covers every loss in between — including losses no single segment can see:

```promql
sum by (bucket) (otel_completeness_acks_total{segment="central-collector"})
  /
sum by (bucket) (otel_completeness_creates_total{segment="daemonset-collector"})
```

**Per segment**, to find out which hop is losing data:

```promql
sum by (bucket) (otel_completeness_acks_total{segment="daemonset-collector"})
  /
sum by (bucket) (otel_completeness_creates_total{segment="daemonset-collector"})
```

**Per hop**, to attribute what is lost *between* two segments — in the network, or inside the next
collector before its own counting starts:

```promql
sum by (bucket) (otel_completeness_creates_total{segment="central-collector"})
  /
sum by (bucket) (otel_completeness_acks_total{segment="daemonset-collector"})
```

**Where a segment lost its records**, from the drop reasons:

```promql
sum by (bucket, reason) (otel_completeness_drops_total{segment="daemonset-collector"})
```

Buckets stay open for as long as records of that bucket are still in flight, so compare buckets that
are older than the maximum time data can spend in the pipeline (queue + retries) to avoid reporting
a shortfall that is only a delay.

These are raw counters, which reset when a collector restarts. Comparing them directly is fine while
the collectors stay up; across restarts, compare the increase over a window that covers the bucket
instead, so that the reset is accounted for:

```promql
sum by (bucket) (increase(otel_completeness_acks_total{segment="central-collector"}[1h]))
  /
sum by (bucket) (increase(otel_completeness_creates_total{segment="daemonset-collector"}[1h]))
```

### Surviving a restart

Records sitting in a non-persistent queue are lost if the collector is killed, and nothing can report
that from a process that is gone. Give the sending queue a [storage extension][queue] and the records
outlive the process: they are restored on startup and counted when they are finally delivered.

```yaml
extensions:
  file_storage:
    directory: /var/lib/otelcol/queue

exporters:
  completeness:
    segment: central-collector
    sending_queue:
      storage: file_storage
    exporter:
      type: clickhouse
      config:
        endpoint: tcp://clickhouse:9000

service:
  extensions: [file_storage]
```

The bucket travels with the records through the queue, so a record enqueued before a restart is
still counted against the minute it was originally stamped with.

### Partial success responses

An OTLP backend may accept a batch while rejecting some of its records. Exporters that report those
records back — as a `consumererror.Logs` — are handled: the rejected records are counted as
`partially_rejected` drops and only the rest is acknowledged.

The collector's own OTLP exporter is not one of them. It writes a `Partial success response` warning
to the log and returns success, discarding which records were rejected, so nothing wrapping it can
tell. On that hop the acknowledgments of the sending segment over-count by the rejected records —
which is exactly what the end-to-end and per-hop ratios above expose, because the receiving segment
only ever counts the records that really arrived.

### What is still outside the count

An exporter that answers before its backend did cannot be corrected from the outside. The sending
queue is the usual case and it is taken over, and a wrapped exporter without one produces a warning
at startup, but an exporter that buffers internally will acknowledge early.

## Cardinality

The bucket ends up as a metric attribute, so its granularity directly determines the cardinality of
the metric: one series per bucket per segment. Truncate to 1 minute or coarser, and never stamp an
untruncated timestamp. Metrics backends keep those series around for their retention period, so a
1-minute bucket over 24 hours means 1440 series per segment.

Since the exporter reads the bucket from the data, a marker set by something other than your own
`transform` statement also ends up as a metric attribute. Only use it on pipelines where the marker
is set by the collector itself, and pick a `bucket_attribute` that upstream services do not write.
